title: Lamp of beauty
hook: the Jaap moves into Persian: He is the glorious one, the lamp of beauty (Jaap)

segments.voice: Yesterday, naad, the sound within sounds, and your line, the dance of dances. Today, Jaap changes language in the middle of the hymn.

A friend who speaks three languages is telling you a story in English. Then they reach the part they really care about, and suddenly it's Spanish, or Punjabi, or Tagalog. Some things only sound right in one language: grandma's words, the word for that kind of evening. Partway through Jaap Sahib, the Tenth Guru does something like that. He moves into Persian, the language of poets and courts, and starts talking about beauty.
screen: `A FRIEND SWITCHES LANGUAGES.` → `SOME THINGS SOUND RIGHT IN ONE.` → `JAAP SWITCHES INTO PERSIAN.`

segments.voice: In the Tenth Guru's world, Persian was the language of the Mughal court, of government papers, and of a great tradition of love poetry. The Guru knew it well; his letter to the emperor, the Zafarnama, is written in it. So when Jaap moves into Persian and Arabic words, it isn't showing off. It reaches for a language with a long habit of praising beauty. The lines begin with a little word, ki, meaning something like: for You are. One of them says the One is husnal charaag. Husn is beauty, the same word Punjabi still uses for a lovely face or a lovely view. Charaag, or chiragh, is a small oil lamp of the kind that lit houses and shrines. The lamp of beauty. A lamp isn't beautiful because of its own shape; it's beautiful because it lets you see everything else. Lamplight makes a room golden. So the line suggests that beauty itself has a source, and that every lovely thing is lit by it. In the same Persian stretch, Jaap uses names like kareem, generous, and raheem, merciful, names Muslims also use for God. The Tenth Guru brings them into Sikh morning prayer without hesitating. Jaap reaches for every language the Guru had, Braj, Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, as if to say: no single tongue holds the One, and every tongue can praise.
screen: `PERSIAN: THE LANGUAGE OF COURTS AND POETS.` · `HUSN: BEAUTY. CHARAAG: A LAMP.` · `A LAMP LETS YOU SEE EVERYTHING ELSE.` · `KAREEM AND RAHEEM: SHARED NAMES.` · then, large: `LAMP OF BEAUTY.`

segments.voice: Find one beautiful thing near you, the grain in a table, light on a wall, the curve of a mug handle, someone's handwriting, and rest your eyes on it. Then notice the light that's letting you see it, a window, a lamp, a screen's glow, and breathe slowly with the two together. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, the word of wonder.
Husnal charaag. Husn is beauty; charaag, a lamp — the One as the lamp that lets every lovely thing be seen.
Your line: makes a room golden. The lamp is what lets the beauty show. Day three hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Jaap Sahib move through its Persian and Arabic passages each morning in the same rhythm as the rest, and the words husn (beauty) and charaag (lamp) are still familiar in Punjabi.

chat.says: Why would a Sikh prayer switch into Persian and call God a lamp?
options: Persian had a long habit of praising beauty; the One is the lamp that lets beauty be seen.
The Guru wanted to impress the Mughal court, so he wrote this part for them.
Persian was the only language holy enough for prayer in the Guru's time.
